% =====================================================================
\section*{Abstract}
% =====================================================================

Linguistic dating of ancient texts rests on an assumption that has never been
measured: that a late author cannot convincingly imitate an earlier stage of
the language.  If imitation is cheap, every early date is worthless.  This
paper measures the price of imitation, and uses a model calibrated against that
price to place the Pentateuchal sources in time.  Features are extracted from
\HBwords{} words of independently anchored Biblical Hebrew --- \HBbooks{}
prophetic and post-exilic books whose dates rest on synchronisms with Assyrian,
Babylonian and Persian records --- partitioned into \HBchunks{} passages of
about 500 words so that high-frequency morphosyntax can be estimated within
each passage rather than only across whole books.  A date model over
\HBfeat{} features, weighted to counteract the corpus's post-exilic skew and
variance-matched so that its output spans the range of real dates, achieves a
leave-one-book-out mean absolute error of \HBmae{}~yr against \HBmaebase{}~yr
for the constant predictor, a rank correlation of $\HBrho$ with true date, and
correct chronological ordering of \HBpair\% of \HBnpair{} book pairs; a
permutation null that re-runs the entire pipeline on shuffled dates gives
$p = \HBpermrho$.  Applied to the documentary sources with distribution-free
conformal intervals, the model places the Priestly, Deuteronomic and JE
composites after the exile with probability $\geq \srcminpost$, and recovers
the classical relative sequence JE $\rightarrow$ D $\rightarrow$ P without
having been trained on any of them.  The archaizing question is then measured rather than
assumed away, in two experiments that give sharply different answers.
Replacing every Late Biblical Hebrew form in six securely dated late books
with its Classical counterpart --- total lexical archaizing, beyond what any
scribe sustains --- moves their estimated dates by a mean of only
\arcMean~yr, because no single lexical item is worth more than
\sensTopLever~yr per standard deviation and the model's remaining leverage
sits in morphology and syntax.  But in Ancient Greek, where archaizing was
practised rather than simulated, the Second Sophistic Atticizers ---
professional imitators of Classical Attic trained in a formal curriculum of
Attic prose composition --- are displaced by a mean of \GKattshift~yr under a
model trained only on non-archaizing Greek, with \GKattearly{} of \GKatt{}
placed earlier than they were written.  The price of archaizing therefore
depends entirely on its mechanism: substituting archaic vocabulary is cheap
and nearly undetectable in its effect on date, while reconstructing an archaic
grammar is expensive to perform and can move an estimate by centuries.  This
reframes the standing objection to linguistic dating.  An archaizing
explanation for an apparently early Hebrew text requires sustained
morphosyntactic imitation of a kind for which the Second Temple period offers
no attested institutional support, not the lexical substitution the
Classical/Late Biblical Hebrew literature describes.  Code and data are
publicly available.

% =====================================================================
\section*{Introduction}
% =====================================================================

Scholars in biblical studies, classical philology, and Near Eastern
linguistics routinely use internal linguistic evidence to constrain the dates
of ancient texts.  The transition from Classical Biblical Hebrew (\cbh{}; also
called Standard Biblical Hebrew) to Late Biblical Hebrew (\lbh{}) is among the
best-documented diachronic shifts in any ancient
language~\cite{Hurvitz1982,Rooker1990,Polzin1976}, and comparable transitions
are well attested in Ancient Greek~\cite{Horrocks2010} and Akkadian.  Despite
this rich empirical tradition, linguistic dating almost never produces
calibrated probability estimates; scholars identify features as ``archaic'' or
``late'' and assign texts to qualitative categories, but the resulting claims
carry no quantified uncertainty.

Underneath the practice sits an assumption that is stated often and tested
never.  The whole enterprise presupposes that a late author cannot
convincingly write like an early one.  If deliberate archaizing were easy ---
if a Persian-period scribe could adopt Classical vocabulary and thereby
acquire a Classical date --- then every linguistic argument for the antiquity
of a biblical text would be worthless, and the objection would apply with
equal force to computational and traditional methods.  The dialectal school
has pressed exactly this point for two
decades~\cite{Young2008,Rezetko2014}, and the mainstream reply has been that
sustained archaizing is difficult.  Both positions are assertions.  Neither
side has put a number on it.

This paper puts a number on it, in two independent ways, and then uses a model
whose archaizing sensitivity is known to place the Pentateuchal sources in
time.  The two contributions are of equal weight, and the second is what makes
the first worth believing.

\textbf{Contribution 1: calibrated date ranges.}  We build a date model on
\HBwords{} words of independently anchored Hebrew, partitioned into
\HBchunks{} passages of about 500 words.  The partition matters more than it
sounds: at book level the corpus supplies \HBbooks{} observations for hundreds
of candidate features, a regime in which nothing can be estimated honestly.
At passage level the same corpus supplies \HBchunks{} observations, and the
features that survive are the high-frequency morphological and syntactic rates
that can actually be measured in a few hundred words.  The model reports
distribution-free conformal intervals rather than point dates, and its
intervals are calibrated on out-of-sample residuals rather than assumed.

\textbf{Contribution 2: the price of archaizing.}  We then measure what the
model can be fooled by, twice, by two routes that turn out to disagree
informatively.  Because we can perform archaizing ourselves, the ground truth
is known exactly: we take securely dated \emph{late} books, replace their
\lbh{} forms with \cbh{} counterparts at controlled rates, re-extract every
feature from the altered text, and re-date it with a model that never saw it.
This prices the \emph{lexical} mechanism, and the price is low.  Separately,
Ancient Greek supplies what Hebrew cannot --- a set of texts whose authors
really did archaize, deliberately and expertly, with securely known
composition dates.  The Second Sophistic Atticizers wrote imitation Classical
Attic four to seven centuries after the Classical period, taught by a formal
curriculum, and their imitation was good enough to be read as a stylistic
model for a millennium.  This prices the \emph{morphosyntactic} mechanism, and
the price is an order of magnitude higher.

That contrast is the paper's answer to the standing objection.  Archaizing is
not uniformly cheap or uniformly hard; its cost depends on how deep into the
grammar the imitation goes, and the two depths are separated by roughly a
factor of twenty in their effect on an estimated date.  Whether a given text
could have been archaized therefore turns on what its author was trained to
do, which is a historical question about scribal education rather than a
statistical one.

The results are bounded in both directions, and we state the bounds plainly.
The model orders books in time far better than chance and places the
Pentateuchal sources after the exile with high probability, but its
\HBqsixeight~yr 68\% intervals are wide, and it should not be read as
resolving dates within the Persian period.  What it does resolve is the
pre-exilic versus post-exilic question, which is the question the Pentateuchal
debate has actually turned on.

The paper is organized as follows.  The Background section reviews the
CBH/LBH distinction, the dialectal challenge, and the circularity problem.
The Data section describes the anchored corpus, the passage-level design, and
feature extraction.  The Model section presents the weighted ridge estimator,
the variance-matching step, and conformal intervals.  The Validation section
documents a failure mode that inflates reported accuracy in this literature,
then reports leave-one-book-out performance against a permutation null.  The
Results section dates the undated units.  The Archaizing section reports both
measurements.  The Discussion addresses limitations and scholarly context.

% =====================================================================
\section*{Background: diachronic Biblical Hebrew}
% =====================================================================

\subsection*{The CBH/LBH distinction}

Classical Biblical Hebrew (\cbh{}) is the language of the pre-exilic prophetic
corpus and early narrative material (8th--7th centuries BCE): Amos, Hosea,
early Isaiah, and the narrative strands of Samuel--Kings.  Late Biblical
Hebrew (\lbh{}) characterizes the post-exilic prose of Ezra, Nehemiah,
Chronicles, Esther, and Daniel (5th--2nd centuries BCE).

The transition is marked by well-studied lexical, morphological, and syntactic
changes~\cite{Hurvitz1997,Rooker1990,Polzin1976,Young2003}.  At the lexical
level, the first-person singular pronoun shifts from \textit{ank\={\i}} to
\textit{an\={\i}}; the relative pronoun \textit{ašer} gives way to the enclitic
\textit{š}e-; the negator \textit{l\={o}\textquotesingle} is supplemented by
and partly replaced by \textit{\textquotesingle \={e}n}.  At the morphological
level, the wayyiqtol declines in frequency while the \textit{h\={a}y\={a}h} +
participle periphrastic increases.  At the syntactic level,
infinitive-absolute constructions rise, and sentence structure shifts toward
analytic patterns associated with Aramaic
influence~\cite{Young2008,Rezetko2014}.

The consensus
view~\cite{Hurvitz1982,Hurvitz2014,Robertson1972,Schniedewind2004} holds that
these features shift monotonically along the temporal axis, constituting a
reliable if noisy diachronic signal.  The present study adopts this view as a
working assumption and then tests the principal alternative to it directly.

\subsection*{The diachronic versus dialectal debate}

Young, Rezetko, and Ehrensv\"{a}rd~\cite{Young2008} argue that the CBH/LBH
contrast may reflect geographic dialect, scribal tradition, or literary
register rather than chronology.  The Qumran sectarian texts
($\sim$150~BCE) deliberately employ \cbh{} vocabulary and morphology while
simultaneously using Aramaic loan-words --- a pattern they interpret as
literary register rather than temporal reality.  Hurvitz and the diachronic
mainstream~\cite{Hurvitz1997} counter that the dialectal alternatives require
additional auxiliary hypotheses, and that the Qumran archaism case
presupposes the original \cbh{} features had already receded, confirming
rather than undermining the diachronic interpretation.

This debate has been conducted almost entirely through argument.  Its
empirical core is a quantitative question --- how much apparent antiquity does
deliberate archaizing actually purchase? --- and that question is answerable.
A model that assigns dates can be fed texts whose archaizing status is known,
either because the archaizing was performed by the investigator or because the
author's imitative program is a matter of literary-historical record.  The
Archaizing section reports both experiments.  We regard this as the
substantive contribution of the paper to the dialectal debate: not a
resolution of it, but a measurement that either side can now argue from.

\subsection*{The circularity problem}

Dating methods that use features identified by comparing texts of assumed date
risk circularity: the assumed dates shape the feature set, and the feature set
is then used to infer unknown dates.  Three safeguards are adopted.

First, the training corpus is restricted to books with \emph{independent}
historical anchoring via synchronisms with datable rulers in Assyrian,
Babylonian, and Persian king-lists.  Torah texts are excluded from training
entirely, so all Torah date estimates are genuine out-of-sample predictions.

Second, no feature is selected using date information.  The feature set is
fixed in advance by frequency rank in the corpus as a whole (Data section),
not by correlation with date.  Feature-by-date screening was evaluated and
rejected: at this dimensionality the false discovery proportion among
screened features is high enough that screening manufactures apparent signal
(S2 Table).

Third, all reported performance comes from leave-one-\emph{book}-out
cross-validation in which standardisation, weighting, regularisation-parameter
selection and interval calibration are performed inside each fold, and
significance is established by a permutation null that re-runs the entire
pipeline on shuffled dates.

\textbf{Why an anchored corpus.}  The Hebrew prophetic books offer a form of
historical anchoring available nowhere else in the Hebrew Bible: their
superscriptions and internal chronological notices can be cross-checked
against records entirely external to the biblical tradition.  Ezekiel
explicitly dates thirteen of his visions to regnal years of the Babylonian
exile --- ``the fifth year of King Jehoiachin's captivity'' (Ezek~1:2), ``the
sixth year'' (8:1), and so forth --- which correlate with Babylonian
administrative texts independently dating Jehoiachin's deportation to
597~BCE.  Other eighth- and seventh-century prophets (Amos, Hosea, Isaiah,
Micah, Zephaniah, Nahum) are anchored by superscriptions naming Judahite and
Israelite kings whose reigns are documented in the Assyrian and
Neo-Babylonian annals.  No comparable external anchoring exists for the Torah
or the poetic books: their dates derive entirely from literary-critical
argument, which is precisely the circularity this study seeks to avoid.

\textbf{Asymmetric error and conservative upper bounds on antiquity.}  If the
accepted dates for the anchored training texts were wrong, the error would be
asymmetric: these texts can be \emph{no older} than the historical events they
reference, but they could in principle be \emph{younger}.  A training corpus
misdated in the direction of being too early would calibrate the
feature-to-date mapping at too early a point on the temporal axis, so unknown
texts dated against that calibration would also be estimated as too early.
Any systematic error in the training dates therefore propagates in a single
direction: all model-derived dates shift toward greater recency.  The dates
reported here should be read as \emph{conservative upper bounds on
antiquity}.  A text dated to 400~BCE may be more recent; the linguistic
evidence provides no support for a date earlier than the estimate.

\subsection*{Prior computational work: attribution versus dating}

Computational approaches to textual attribution and stylometric dating have a
substantial history, from Mosteller and Wallace's Bayesian analysis of the
Federalist Papers~\cite{Mosteller1984} through the stylometric tradition
surveyed by Holmes~\cite{Holmes1998} and the function-word methods of
Burrows~\cite{Burrows2002}.  Among work applied specifically to the Hebrew
Bible, Faigenbaum-Golovin et al.~\cite{Faigenbaum2025} provide the most
methodologically rigorous prior computational treatment.  Their Higher
Criticism discrepancy method tests whether the distribution of lemma n-gram
frequencies in a target text deviates from the null that it was produced by
the same process as a reference corpus.  Applied to 50 ground-truth chapters
spanning D, the Deuteronomistic History, and P, it achieves 84\% attribution
accuracy in leave-one-out validation and yields interpretable discriminating
lemma lists.

The present framework answers a different question, and three differences
follow from that.

\textbf{Continuous dates versus categorical assignment.}  The Higher Criticism
method assigns each text to the most likely of three corpora.  Because D and
the Deuteronomistic History are both dated to the late monarchic or exilic
period, two texts composed at 650 and 590~BCE receive identical labels; no
intra-school temporal resolution is possible.  The model used here returns a
date with a calibrated interval, recovering whatever temporal resolution the
data support and quantifying the rest as uncertainty.

\textbf{Period features versus topic features.}  Faigenbaum-Golovin et al.\
operate on lemma and lemma n-gram frequencies, a representation in which
content words --- \textit{gold} in Tabernacle chapters, \textit{king} in
regnal narratives --- dominate.  Content-word frequency is sensitive to topic
and genre as much as to date.  The feature set here is deliberately dominated
by high-frequency grammatical rates (verbal aspect and stem distributions,
part-of-speech transition rates, clause-relation profiles) that vary with
period rather than subject matter.  This is what permits comparison of poetry
against narrative, which a bag-of-words representation cannot do.

\textbf{A measured archaizing sensitivity.}  Attribution methods offer no
mechanism for distinguishing a genuinely ancient text from one composed in a
deliberately archaic register: a Persian-period author who archaizes to D
norms is assigned to D regardless of composition date.  Rather than claim
immunity, we measure the sensitivity directly and report it as a quantity
(Archaizing section).  A reader who believes archaizing was widespread can
take the measured exchange rate and compute for themselves how much of any
reported date it could account for.

These are differences of purpose rather than deficiencies in either approach.
The ideal analysis of a disputed text would apply both: attribution output can
set register priors, and date estimates constrain the plausible compositional
settings for attribution decisions.

% =====================================================================
\section*{Data: corpus and feature extraction}
% =====================================================================

\subsection*{The BHSA database}

All Hebrew analysis uses the Biblia Hebraica Stuttgartensia Amstelodamensis
(\bhsa{}) database~\cite{BHSA2021}, accessed through
Text-Fabric~\cite{Roorda2018}.  \bhsa{} supplies a complete morphological and
syntactic annotation of the Masoretic text: for every word, a lexeme
identifier, part of speech, verbal tense/aspect and stem, person, number,
gender, pronominal suffix and state; and for every phrase and clause, a type,
a syntactic function, and a relation to its governing clause.  These
annotations are the product of decades of work by the Eep Talstra Centre for
Bible and Computer and are independent of any dating hypothesis.

\subsection*{Training corpus}

The training corpus comprises \HBbooks{} units spanning \HBoldest--\HBlatest{}
BCE, listed with their anchors in Table~\ref{tab:corpus}.  Every date rests on
a synchronism external to the biblical tradition or on an event whose date is
fixed by external record.  Books with disputed internal composition
histories are split into the conventional scholarly divisions (Isaiah into
three, Zechariah into two) and the oracular core of Jeremiah is separated from
its Deuteronomistic prose frame, which is treated as an undated target rather
than an anchor.

\input{tables/tab_corpus}

\subsection*{Passage-level design}

The single most consequential design choice in this paper is that features are
extracted from passages of about 500 words rather than from whole books.

At book level the corpus offers \HBbooks{} observations.  Any feature set
large enough to describe Hebrew morphosyntax then has more dimensions than
there are data points, and the standard responses --- screening features by
their correlation with date, or reducing dimension using the date labels ---
both use the labels before cross-validation and inflate apparent performance.
Worse, a whole-book rate is a single number summarising tens of thousands of
words, so the model cannot distinguish a book whose passages are internally
consistent from one that is a composite.

Partitioning at $\sim$500 words yields \HBchunks{} passages from the same
\HBwords{} words.  The gain is not a free multiplication of sample size:
passages from one book are correlated, and the appropriate measure is the
effective sample size $n_{\mathrm{eff}} = n / (1 + (\bar{m}-1)\rho_{I})$ where
$\rho_I$ is the intraclass correlation and $\bar m$ the mean passages per
book.  Across chunk sizes from 200 to 1000 words the median intraclass
correlation runs 0.20--0.32 and the resulting effective sample size is three
to seven times the book-level figure (S2 Table).  That is the honest gain, and
it is what makes a feature set of this width estimable at all.

Passage size trades two effects against each other.  Smaller passages give
more observations but sparser features: a lexical item occurring once per
thousand words is absent from most 200-word passages, and its rate is then not
a measurement but a coin flip.  Larger passages give denser features but fewer
observations.  We searched passage sizes of 200, 300, 400, 500, 700 and 1000
words crossed with three feature sets and with calibration on and off, 36
configurations in all, selecting on out-of-sample rank correlation under
leave-one-book-out (S3 Table).  The selected configuration uses $\sim$500-word
passages; performance is flat between 400 and 1000, so the choice is not
delicate.

Passages respect verse boundaries: words are accumulated verse by verse until
the target is reached.  A trailing remainder shorter than half the target is
merged into the preceding passage rather than kept as a short, high-variance
observation.

\subsection*{Feature extraction}

The feature set is fixed by frequency rank computed over the whole \bhsa{}
corpus, without reference to date.  It comprises \HBfeat{} features in six
families:

\begin{enumerate}
  \item \textbf{Lexical rates} (250 features): occurrences per 1000 words of
    each of the 250 most frequent lexemes in the corpus.  Because selection is
    by corpus frequency, these are dominated by function words --- articles,
    prepositions, conjunctions, pronouns --- rather than by the rare
    diagnostic vocabulary of the \cbh{}/\lbh{} literature.  This is
    deliberate; the sparsity constraint above rules out the rare items, and
    the Archaizing section shows the consequence.
  \item \textbf{Part-of-speech transition rates} (207 features): rates of each
    ordered pair of parts of speech across adjacent words, capturing local
    syntactic profile without reference to any particular construction.
  \item \textbf{Verb morphology} (57 features): distributions over tense/aspect
    (qatal, yiqtol, wayyiqtol, participle, infinitive, imperative), stem (qal,
    nifal, piel, hifil, hitpael, pual, hofal), and their interaction.
  \item \textbf{Phrase and clause structure} (40 features): phrase type and
    syntactic function rates, and clause-relation rates from the \bhsa{}
    clause hierarchy.
  \item \textbf{Agreement and suffix morphology} (20 features): person, number,
    gender and pronominal-suffix rates.
  \item \textbf{Structural} (5 features): mean phrase and clause length,
    clauses per passage, and type--token ratio.
\end{enumerate}

A character and part-of-speech n-gram extension adding 689 further features
was built and evaluated (S3 Table).  It does not improve out-of-sample
performance at the selected passage size and is not used in the reported
model; it is retained in the repository for replication.

Features whose standard deviation is zero on the training fold, or which are
missing in more than 20\% of passages, are dropped inside the fold.  Remaining
missing values are imputed at the training-fold median.

% =====================================================================
\section*{Model}
% =====================================================================

\subsection*{Weighted ridge regression}

Let $\mathbf{X}$ be the $n \times p$ matrix of passage features and
$\mathbf{y}$ the vector of book dates, each passage inheriting its book's
date.  Features are centred and scaled on the training fold.  The estimator is
ridge regression,
\begin{equation}
\hat{\boldsymbol\beta}
  = \arg\min_{\boldsymbol\beta}
    \sum_{i=1}^{n} w_i \left( y_i - \mathbf{x}_i^{\!\top}\boldsymbol\beta \right)^2
    + \lambda \|\boldsymbol\beta\|^2 ,
\end{equation}
solved in dual form, $\hat{\boldsymbol\beta} =
\mathbf{A}^{\!\top}(\mathbf{A}\mathbf{A}^{\!\top} + \lambda\mathbf{I})^{-1}
\tilde{\mathbf{y}}$, where $\mathbf{A}$ is the weighted standardised design.
Because $p > n$ on the Hebrew side, the dual form is the cheaper route, and
one eigendecomposition of $\mathbf{A}\mathbf{A}^{\!\top}$ serves the entire
$\lambda$ sweep.  $\lambda$ is selected by an inner leave-one-book-out loop
nested inside each outer fold, never using the held-out book.

\subsection*{Inverse-density weighting}

The anchored corpus is not uniform in time.  Post-exilic material outnumbers
pre-exilic material, and an unweighted fit is pulled toward the dense region:
in the unweighted model no book receives a confidently pre-exilic estimate,
which is a property of the sampling rather than of Hebrew.  Weights are
therefore taken inversely proportional to a kernel estimate of the date
density,
\begin{equation}
w_i \propto \left[ \sum_j \exp\!\left( -\tfrac{1}{2}
  \left( \frac{d_j - d_i}{h} \right)^{\!2} \right) \right]^{-\alpha} ,
\end{equation}
with bandwidth $h = 90$~yr and exponent $\alpha = 1$, normalised to mean one.
Weighted ridge is implemented as ordinary ridge on rows scaled by
$\sqrt{w_i}$.

\subsection*{Variance matching, and what it costs}

A regularised regression is a shrinkage estimator: its predictions have
systematically smaller variance than the quantity being predicted.  Under
plain ridge the predicted dates for the anchored corpus span roughly a third
of the true range, so no text can be assigned a confidently early or
confidently late date --- an artifact of shrinkage, not a finding about
Hebrew.  We correct it by matching the first two moments of the
out-of-sample predictions to the true dates,
\begin{equation}
\hat{d} \;=\; \bar{d} \;+\; S\,(\hat{d}_{\text{raw}} - \bar{d}_{\text{raw}}),
\qquad
S = \frac{\mathrm{sd}(d)}{\mathrm{sd}(\hat{d}_{\text{raw}})},
\end{equation}
with $\bar d$, $\mathrm{sd}(d)$, $\bar d_{\text{raw}}$ and $S$ all computed
from leave-one-book-out predictions on the training corpus only.  Here
$S = \HBscale$.

This is a deliberate trade, and we report both sides of it.  Rescaling
\emph{increases} mean absolute error: the uncalibrated model achieves
\UNCALmae~yr against \HBmae~yr for the rescaled one, because inflating the
spread of predictions amplifies their errors along with their signal.  What
it buys is a model that is two-sided.  Uncalibrated predictions span only
\UNCALspan~yr against \TRUEspan~yr of real dates, and place just \UNCALpreok{}
of the \HBnpre{} genuinely pre-exilic books before the exile; after rescaling
the predictions span \VARspan~yr and \HBnpreok{} of \HBnpre{} are placed
correctly.

Since the substantive question in the Pentateuchal debate is which side of the
exile a text falls on, a model that can hardly ever say ``early'' is useless
for it whatever its mean absolute error --- and its inability to say ``early''
is a property of the estimator, not evidence that nothing is early.  A reader
whose interest is point accuracy rather than calibration should use the
uncalibrated variant; its figures are in S3 Table.

\subsection*{Conformal prediction intervals}

Intervals are conformal, calibrated on the absolute leave-one-book-out
residuals of the rescaled predictions.  For coverage level $1-\alpha$ the
half-width is the $\lceil (n+1)(1-\alpha) \rceil$-th smallest absolute
residual.  This is distribution-free and has finite-sample marginal
coverage~\cite{Vovk2005,Lei2018}: it assumes only that the target text is
exchangeable with the anchored corpus, not that residuals are Gaussian or
homoscedastic.  On this corpus the half-widths are $\pm\HBqsixeight$~yr at
68\% and $\pm\HBqninety$~yr at 90\%.

For a target unit, $P(\text{post-exilic})$ is computed by adding the empirical
residual distribution to the point estimate and taking the fraction of the
resulting draws that fall after 586~BCE.  This inherits the conformal
guarantee and makes no distributional assumption.

% =====================================================================
\section*{Validation}
\label{sec:validation}
% =====================================================================

\subsection*{A failure mode that inflates reported accuracy}

Reported accuracies for linguistic dating models of this class vary by two
orders of magnitude, and part of the variation is a design artifact worth
naming, because we committed it ourselves in an earlier version of this work.

In a Bayesian dating model the posterior over a held-out text's date combines
a likelihood from the linguistic features with a prior.  If the prior for the
held-out text is centred on that text's own scholarly date --- which is the
natural thing to do when the prior encodes ``what scholars think'' --- then
the model is being asked to recover a number it has already been given.  The
resulting holdout error measures the width of the prior, not the information
in the language.

The effect is large.  Under a prior-centred design on this corpus, the median
share of posterior precision contributed by the linguistic evidence is
\leakShare\%, and mean holdout error is \leakLeaky~yr.  Under an agnostic
prior with an otherwise identical pipeline, the same model achieves
\leakHonest~yr.  For the \leakTightN{} units whose scholarly dates carry the
tightest uncertainty ($\sigma \leq 20$~yr), the linguistic evidence supplies
\leakTightShare\% of posterior precision and the leaky design reports
\leakTightLeaky~yr against an honest \leakTightHonest~yr
(Table~\ref{tab:leakage}).  A reported accuracy of a decade or two, for a
model of this kind, is a signature of the design rather than an achievement.

\input{tables/tab_leakage}

All results below use an agnostic prior; the reported model is not Bayesian
and has no prior to leak.

\subsection*{Leave-one-book-out protocol}

Cross-validation folds are whole books, never passages.  Passages from one
book are strongly correlated, so splitting them across the fold boundary would
let the model see the held-out book's own material.  Inside each fold, and
using only the training books: features with zero variance or excessive
missingness are dropped; medians for imputation are computed; standardisation
constants are computed; inverse-density weights are computed; $\lambda$ is
selected by an inner leave-one-book-out loop; and the variance-matching
constants and conformal residuals are derived.  The held-out book's date is
used only to score the result.

A book's estimate is the median of its passage estimates.  The dispersion of
passage estimates within a book is reported separately (Table~\ref{tab:lobo})
and is informative in its own right: it is small for compositionally uniform
books and large for composites.

\subsection*{What the signal supports}

\input{tables/tab_lobo}

Under this protocol the model achieves a mean absolute error of \HBmae~yr,
against \HBmaebase~yr for the constant predictor that assigns every book the
corpus mean date.  Rank correlation between true and estimated date is
$\HBrho$ ($p = \HBrhop$), and \HBpair\% of the \HBnpair{} book pairs are
placed in the correct chronological order.

Because the same corpus was used to choose the passage size and feature set,
parametric $p$-values would be optimistic.  Significance is therefore
established by a permutation null in which book dates are shuffled and the
\emph{entire} pipeline is re-run --- weighting, $\lambda$ selection, variance
matching and all --- \HBnperm{} times.  Permutation is at book level, not
passage level, so the clustering structure is preserved under the null; a
passage-level shuffle would break the correlation between passages of the same
book and produce a null that is far too easy to beat.  Against this null the
observed rank correlation of $\HBrho$ has $p = \HBpermrho$ (null median
$\HBnullrho$), the pairwise ordering accuracy of \HBpair\% has $p =
\HBpermpair$ (null median \HBnullpair\%), and the mean absolute error of
\HBmae~yr has $p = \HBpermmae$ (null median \HBnullmae~yr).

We flag one arithmetic trap explicitly, having fallen into it.  The
\HBnpair{} pairs formed from \HBbooks{} books are not independent: each book
appears in \HBbooks$-1$ of them.  Treating pairwise ordering accuracy as a
binomial proportion over \HBnpair{} independent trials produces $p$-values
wrong by ten orders of magnitude.  The permutation figures above are the
correct ones.

\subsection*{Two-sidedness and calibration}

The property that matters for the Pentateuchal application is whether the
model can say ``early'' as well as ``late''.  After inverse-density weighting
and variance matching, \HBnpreok{} of the \HBnpre{} genuinely pre-exilic books
are placed before 586~BCE and \HBnpostok{} of the \HBnpost{} genuinely
post-exilic books after it, for \HBsideok/\HBbooks{} overall
(Table~\ref{tab:lobo}).  Without those two steps the model places essentially
nothing before the exile, and its apparent confidence that everything is late
is an artifact of the corpus's date distribution rather than evidence about
any text.

Fig~\ref{fig:calibration} shows estimated against true date with the conformal
bands.  Empirical coverage of the nominal 68\% band is slightly conservative,
which is the expected behaviour of conformal intervals at this sample size.

\begin{figure}[!ht]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=0.62\textwidth]{figures/fig_calibration.pdf}
\caption{{\bf Leave-one-book-out calibration.}  Each point is one anchored
book, dated by a model fitted without it.  The dashed line is exact recovery;
shaded bands are the 68\% and 90\% conformal intervals.  Books whose estimate
falls on the wrong side of the exile are marked with diamonds.  Standardisation,
weighting, regularisation and interval calibration were all performed inside
the fold.}
\label{fig:calibration}
\end{figure}

\subsection*{What the signal does not support}

Three limits deserve statement in the same breath as the results.

First, \HBmae~yr against a \HBmaebase~yr baseline is a real but modest
improvement.  The model is a chronological \emph{ordering} device that has
been calibrated onto an absolute scale; it is not a precise clock.  Reported
intervals of $\pm\HBqsixeight$~yr at 68\% are the honest expression of that.

Second, the largest single error is \HBworstbook{} at \HBworsterr~yr.  Genre
is the main driver: relative to their true dates, narrative books are placed
late and poetic books early (Results section).  Any single estimate for a text
of unusual genre should be read with that in mind.

Third, nothing here resolves dates \emph{within} the post-exilic period.  A
text estimated at 380~BCE with a $\pm\HBqsixeight$~yr interval is not
distinguishable from one estimated at 300~BCE.  Claims below are confined to
the pre-exilic/post-exilic distinction and to relative ordering, both of which
the validation supports.

% =====================================================================
\section*{Results: dating the undated units}
\label{sec:results}
% =====================================================================

The model, fitted on all \HBbooks{} anchored books, was applied to
\NTargets{} undated units: the three classical documentary sources, their
conventional sub-strata, the five Pentateuchal books as received, the
Deuteronomistic prose of Jeremiah, and the three archaic poems.  Source
partitions follow the standard critical division, specified by chapter and
verse in S1 Appendix.  No target contributed to training, feature selection,
weighting, regularisation or calibration.

\input{tables/tab_targets}

\subsection*{The documentary sources are post-exilic}

The Priestly source is placed at \srcP{} BCE (68\% conformal interval
\srcPlo--\srcPhi{} BCE) with $P(\text{post-exilic}) = \srcPpost$; the
Deuteronomic source at \srcD{} BCE (\srcDlo--\srcDhi) with \srcDpost; and the
JE composite at \srcJE{} BCE (\srcJElo--\srcJEhi) with \srcJEpost{}
(Fig~\ref{fig:targets}).  All three fall after the exile with probability at
least \srcminpost.

\begin{figure}[!ht]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=0.92\textwidth]{figures/fig_targets.pdf}
\caption{{\bf Undated units with conformal intervals.}  Thick bars are 68\%
intervals, thin bars 90\%; the dashed line is the exile of 586~BCE.  Colour
marks which side of the exile the point estimate falls on.  The three poems
are extracted at verse precision.  No unit shown contributed to training,
feature selection, weighting, regularisation or calibration.}
\label{fig:targets}
\end{figure}

The relative ordering is JE $\rightarrow$ D $\rightarrow$ P, the classical
sequence of the documentary hypothesis, recovered from linguistic evidence
alone by a model trained only on independently anchored prophetic and
post-exilic books.  We stress that the \emph{ordering} is the better-supported
result: given \HBqsixeight~yr intervals, the three sources' ranges overlap
substantially, and the ordering claim rests on the model's demonstrated
ordering ability rather than on the separation of the point estimates.

\subsection*{Sub-strata}

Splitting Deuteronomy into its law code (chapters 12--26) and its narrative
frame places the code at \srcDCode{} BCE and the frame at \srcDFrame{} BCE ---
the code earlier than the frame, in the direction the critical consensus
expects if the code is the older core around which the frame was later built.
Within Leviticus, the Holiness Code (17--26) is placed at \srcHol{} BCE
against \srcLevP{} BCE for the Priestly material of 1--16.  The JE material of
Genesis, Exodus and Numbers is placed at \srcGenJE, \srcExoJE{} and \srcNumJE{}
BCE respectively.  The Deuteronomistic prose of Jeremiah is placed at
\srcJerD{} BCE.

These sub-strata differences are small relative to the interval width and
should be read as ordering statements consistent with existing
literary-critical arguments rather than as independent confirmation of them.

\subsection*{The archaic poems, and an extraction artifact}

The three poems traditionally regarded as the oldest Hebrew
verse~\cite{Albright1968,Cross1975,Robertson1972} required a correction before
they could be dated at all.

Poems in this corpus are conventionally identified by chapter, but the
chapters containing them also contain prose.  Exodus~15 is
\poemSeaProseFrac\% prose by word count; Deuteronomy~32 is
\poemMosesProseFrac\%.  Because narrative is systematically placed late by
this model, including the prose frame drags the poem's estimate later.  The
effect is not small: the Song of the Sea moves from \poemSeaChap{} BCE when
extracted as a whole chapter to \poemSea{} BCE when extracted at verse
precision (Exod~15:1--18).  We report the verse-precise figures and flag the
chapter-level ones as an artifact, since the same convention is widespread.

At verse precision the Song of the Sea is placed at \poemSea{} BCE
(\poemSealo--\poemSeahi, $P(\text{post-exilic}) = \poemSeapost$) and the Song
of Deborah at \poemDeb{} BCE (\poemDeblo--\poemDebhi, \poemDebpost).  These
are the two earliest of the \NTargets{} undated units, in agreement with a
century of philological argument that they are the oldest surviving Hebrew,
and reached without training on them.

The Song of the Sea's prose continuation (Exod~15:19--27) is placed at
\poemSeaProse{} BCE, \poemSeaGap~yr later than the poem it follows.  A gap of
that size between adjacent verses is itself evidence that the poem is not a
composition of its narrative frame.  The Archaizing section takes up whether
that gap could have been manufactured.

The Song of Moses (Deut~32:1--43) is placed at \poemMoses{} BCE
(\poemMoseslo--\poemMoseshi, \poemMosespost), appreciably later than the other
two and straddling the exile.  This is not what a reading of its content would
predict: its divine-council theology, in which Elyon apportions the nations
among the gods and YHWH receives Israel as his share (32:8--9), is usually
taken as among the most archaic material in the Hebrew Bible.  The model sees
its language, not its theology, and places the language late.  We report the
discrepancy rather than explain it away.

\subsection*{Genre is the dominant confound}

Residuals on the anchored corpus are structured by genre.  Relative to their
true dates, narrative books are placed \emph{late} and poetic books
\emph{early}.  The clearest case is Lamentations, whose date is fixed by its
subject matter --- it laments the destruction of 586~BCE --- and which is
therefore as securely anchored as any text in the corpus.  The model places it
at \lamPred{} BCE against a true \lamTruth{} BCE, an error of \lamErr~yr in
the direction of greater antiquity.  Lamentations is poetry.

This has a direct bearing on the poems above.  If poetry as such is placed
early by this model, then part of the antiquity assigned to the Songs of the
Sea and Deborah may be genre rather than date.  We decline to apply a genre
correction: with a single securely dated poetic book in the anchored corpus,
any correction would be estimated from one observation.  The appropriate
statement is that the poems' early placement is supported by the model but
partially confounded with genre, and that enlarging the anchored poetic corpus
is the way to separate them.

% =====================================================================
\section*{How much antiquity can archaizing buy?}
\label{sec:archaizing}
% =====================================================================

Everything above depends on a premise: that the language of a text reflects
when it was written rather than when its author wished to seem to be writing.
This section measures the size of the gap between those two things, first by
performing archaizing ourselves on Hebrew, then by using Greek texts whose
authors performed it for us.

\subsection*{Synthetic archaizing in Hebrew}

Take a securely dated \emph{late} book, replace its \lbh{} forms with their
\cbh{} counterparts at a controlled rate $r$, re-extract all \HBfeat{}
features from the modified text, and re-date it with a model trained on the
other 24 books.  Because we performed the substitution, the ground truth is
known exactly.

The substitutions are the classical diagnostics of the \cbh{}/\lbh{}
literature, applied in the \lbh{} $\rightarrow$ \cbh{} direction: the relative
particle \textit{še-} $\rightarrow$ \textit{ašer}; the first-person pronoun
\textit{an\={\i}} $\rightarrow$ \textit{ank\={\i}}; \textit{malk\={u}t}
$\rightarrow$ \textit{maml\={a}k\={a}h}; and the negator
\textit{\textquotesingle \={e}n} $\rightarrow$ \textit{l\={o}\textquotesingle},
which changes part of speech as well as lexeme.  Substitution is applied at
the token level before feature extraction, so every downstream feature ---
lexeme rates, part-of-speech transitions, phrase types, clause relations ---
sees the altered text exactly as it would if a scribe had written it that way.
$r$ runs from 0 to 1; at $r = 1$ not one \lbh{} token of these types survives
anywhere in the book.

\input{tables/tab_archaize}

Total lexical archaizing moves the estimated date by a mean of
\arcMean~yr, with a maximum of \arcMax~yr across the \arcN{} books
(Table~\ref{tab:archaize}).  The response is gradual rather than thresholded:
there is no substitution rate at which the estimate jumps.

Three of the six books had almost nothing to substitute --- Ezra offers
\arcEzraTokens{} eligible tokens in the entire book --- so their null results
carry little information; one cannot archaize a text that already lacks the
forms.  Among the \arcInfN{} books with substantial substitution density the
exchange rate is about \arcRate~yr of apparent antiquity per substitution per
1000 words.  Ecclesiastes at $r = 1$ has \arcEccDens{} substitutions per 1000
words --- roughly one word in thirty replaced, a density no scribe sustains
across a book --- and moves \arcEccShift~yr.

\subsection*{Where the model's leverage lives}

The reason for that small number is visible in the model's coefficients.
\begin{figure}[!ht]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=\textwidth]{figures/fig_archaize.pdf}
\caption{{\bf The price of archaizing, by mechanism.}  {\bf A}, Hebrew:
apparent antiquity gained as Late Biblical Hebrew forms are replaced by
Classical counterparts at increasing rates in six securely dated late books.
Solid lines are the books with enough eligible tokens for the result to be
informative.  {\bf B}, Greek: displacement of the Second Sophistic Atticizers
under a model trained only on non-archaizing Greek, with the model's own error
on non-archaizing texts shaded for comparison.  Lexical substitution moves an
estimate by tens of years; reconstructed grammar moves it by hundreds.}
\label{fig:archaize}
\end{figure}

Fig~\ref{fig:leverage} reports the change in estimated date produced by a
one-standard-deviation shift in each feature.  Lexical features carry
\sensLexShare\% of total leverage --- but spread across \sensLexCount{}
features, none worth more than \sensTopLever~yr per standard deviation.  No
single word is a lever.  The remaining leverage sits in part-of-speech
transition rates, verbal aspect and stem distributions, and clause-relation
profiles: high-frequency grammatical habits rather than vocabulary choices.

These are precisely the features that the passage-level design forces the
model to rely on.  Requiring a feature to be measurable within 500 words
demotes the rare diagnostic vocabulary --- which is the manipulable part of
the language --- and promotes high-frequency morphology, which is not.
Resistance to archaizing was not designed into this model; it is a consequence
of the sample-size constraint.

\begin{figure}[!ht]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=0.62\textwidth]{figures/fig_leverage.pdf}
\caption{{\bf Where the model's leverage lives.}  Share of total leverage on
the date estimate by feature family, where leverage is the absolute change in
estimated date produced by a one-standard-deviation shift in a feature, summed
within family.  Lexical features carry the largest share but spread it across
\sensLexCount{} weak features; the majority of leverage sits in morphology and
syntax.}
\label{fig:leverage}
\end{figure}

The quantitative form of the statement: because the model is linear in
standardised features, the smallest coordinated feature shift that displaces an
estimate by $D$ years has length $D/\|\boldsymbol\beta\|$ in standard
deviations.  For the \poemSeaGap~yr gap between the Song of the Sea and its
prose frame, that is \sensSD{} standard deviations across
\sensDim{} dimensions.  Not a word swap --- a systematic re-profiling of the
text's morphology and syntax, sustained across the whole passage.  The Greek
results below show that this is achievable, by authors trained to achieve it.

\subsection*{Greek: archaizing that really happened}

The Hebrew experiment simulates archaizing, and simulates only its lexical
component.  Ancient Greek supplies the real thing, labelled.  During the
Second Sophistic, prose authors of the first three centuries CE deliberately
wrote in imitation of Classical Attic, four to seven centuries after the fact.
The programme was explicit and institutional: Attic prose composition was
taught in the rhetorical schools, dictionaries of permitted Attic usage were
compiled, and the imitation was successful enough that its practitioners were
read as models of style for a millennium.  Their composition dates are
securely known from external evidence.  This is the labelled archaizing set
that Hebrew cannot provide.

We built the same pipeline on a \GKtexts-text corpus of non-archaizing Greek
prose spanning the Classical and Koine periods, partitioned into \GKchunks{}
passages, with \GKfeat{} features.  Greek lacks a morphological annotation
comparable to \bhsa{}, so hand-built morphosyntactic rates (optative,
infinitive and participle rates, particle and negation rates, the
$\tau\tau$ versus $\sigma\sigma$ contrast, sentence length) are supplemented by
word-form, character n-gram and function-word bigram rates --- all
high-frequency by construction, as on the Hebrew side.  Under
leave-one-text-out the Greek model achieves \GKmae~yr against \GKmaebase~yr
for the constant predictor, rank correlation $\GKrho$, and \GKpair\% pairwise
ordering accuracy.  The replication is therefore genuine: the same design
recovers a diachronic signal in an unrelated language.

The \GKatt{} Atticizing texts were excluded from training entirely and then
dated.

\input{tables/tab_greek}

The mean displacement is \GKattshift~yr, with \GKattearly{} of \GKatt{} texts
placed earlier than they were written (Fig~\ref{fig:archaize}B).  \GKattmaxname{}
is displaced \GKattmaxearly~yr.  Set against the model's own \GKmae~yr error
on non-archaizing texts, this is a large effect: deliberate, professionally
trained archaizing displaces a text by more than one full error width, and in
the worst cases by half a millennium.

Two features of the Greek corpus deserve comment because they bear on how the
number should be read.

First, the effect is if anything \emph{understated}, because the training set
is contaminated.  The corpus manifest classifies Aelian, Appian, Diogenes
Laertius, Plotinus, Porphyry, Iamblichus and the sophistic novelists as Koine,
so they were used as non-archaizing training material --- yet every one of
them is described in the literary-historical record as classicizing, and the
model placed them among the largest early displacements in the training set
even though it had been told they were not archaizing.  A training set that
contains archaizers teaches the model that late texts look early, which shrinks
the measured displacement of the declared Atticizers.  Because the
classification is a scholarly judgment rather than a datum, we do not adopt one
and defend it; we report the measurement under three definitions of the
training set --- the manifest's own labels, a stricter classification that
reclassifies the authors named above, and a date-blind variant that discards
register labels entirely and trains only on texts composed before 50~CE, prior
to the Second Sophistic (S6 Table).

The result is robust in sign and grows under stricter definitions: the mean
displacement is \GKattshift~yr under the manifest's labels, \GKattshiftB~yr
under the stricter classification, and \GKattshiftC~yr under the date-blind
variant, with \GKattearlyTot{} of \GKattTot{} individual texts across the three
placed earlier than they were written.  Two things are worth noting about the
stricter variant.  It removes eight texts from training, and yet the model's
own leave-one-text-out error \emph{falls} from \GKmae~yr to \GKmaeB~yr and its
rank correlation rises from $\GKrho$ to $\GKrhoB$ --- removing suspected
archaizers from the training set makes the date model better, which is what
one would expect if they were genuinely mislabelled.  We nonetheless report
the manifest's own labels as the primary specification throughout, because it
is the only one that involves no judgment of ours, and it is the most
conservative.

Second, the two Atticizers displaced least --- Strabo and Dionysius of
Halicarnassus --- are the earliest in the set, writing around the turn of the
era when the Atticizing programme was young.  The displacement grows with the
maturity of the movement, which is what one would expect if it is measuring
imitation rather than noise.

The available texts vary greatly in length, from four passages to five
hundred, and a four-passage estimate is correspondingly noisy.  The result is
not driven by the short texts: weighting each text by its passage count gives
\GKattshiftW~yr, and restricting to the \GKattbign{} texts with at least 40
passages gives \GKattshiftBig~yr, with all \GKattbign{} placed earlier than
they were written.

\subsection*{What the two experiments jointly establish}

The two experiments do not give the same number, and the difference is the
substantive finding.

Total \emph{lexical} archaizing in Hebrew buys \arcMean~yr.  Real
\emph{morphosyntactic} archaizing in Greek buys \GKattshift~yr.  The gap is
roughly an order of magnitude, and it falls exactly where the
feature-leverage analysis said it would.  Swapping diagnostic vocabulary moves
a handful of the \sensLexCount{} weak lexical features and leaves the other
half of the model's leverage untouched.  The Atticizers did not swap
vocabulary; they reconstructed a grammar --- reviving the optative, restoring
the $\mu\acute{\varepsilon}\nu \ldots \delta\acute{\varepsilon}$ articulation,
writing $\tau\tau$ for $\sigma\sigma$, matching Classical participial
density --- which is precisely the coordinated multi-dimensional shift that
the Hebrew sensitivity analysis identified as the only route to a displacement
of centuries.  They achieved it because an entire educational apparatus
existed to teach them how.

The conclusion is therefore conditional rather than absolute, and we state it
in that form.  Archaizing can defeat a model of this class.  What it takes is
not a scribe who knows the old words but a scribe trained to write the old
grammar, sustained across a whole composition.  The relevant question for any
particular text is whether such training existed in its milieu.

For the Hebrew Bible this becomes a historical question rather than a
statistical one, and it is not one this paper settles.  We note only that the
institutional preconditions differ sharply between the two cases: the Second
Sophistic had a documented curriculum of Attic prose composition, lexica of
permitted usage, and a literary culture that rewarded successful imitation,
while no comparable programme of Classical Hebrew prose composition is
attested for the Second Temple period.  The Qumran evidence adduced by the
dialectal school~\cite{Young2008} is the closest analogue and is a good deal
thinner: the sectarian scrolls mix \cbh{} forms with Aramaisms rather than
sustaining a consistent Classical grammar, which on the evidence here would
displace their apparent date by tens of years, not hundreds.

Applied to the results of the previous section, this means the early placement
of the Song of the Sea and the Song of Deborah is not immune to an archaizing
explanation, and we withdraw any such claim.  It means that an archaizing
explanation must posit sustained morphosyntactic imitation of a kind for which
Second Temple Judaism offers no attested institutional support, rather than
the lexical substitution that the \cbh{}/\lbh{} literature actually describes.
That is a weaker defence than immunity, and it is the one the evidence
supports.

% =====================================================================
\section*{Discussion}
% =====================================================================

\subsection*{Limitations}

\textbf{Interval width.}  The 68\% intervals are $\pm\HBqsixeight$~yr and the
90\% intervals $\pm\HBqninety$~yr.  These are honest but wide, and they
preclude any claim about position within the Persian period.  Every
substantive claim above is either a side-of-the-exile claim or an ordering
claim.

\textbf{Genre.}  Poetic texts are placed early and narrative texts late
relative to their true dates.  With one securely dated poetic book in the
anchored corpus, genre cannot be separated from date by this design.  This
directly affects the archaic poems, which are the results most likely to be
cited and are also the ones most exposed to this confound.

\textbf{Corpus asymmetry.}  The anchored corpus is skewed post-exilic, because
that is where external synchronisms are dense.  Inverse-density weighting
mitigates but does not remove the skew, and the pre-exilic end of the scale
rests on \HBnpre{} books.  Extending the anchored corpus at the early end
would do more for this model than any change of estimator.

\textbf{The two archaizing measurements bound different things.}  Four
substitution pairs is a small vocabulary of archaizing, so the Hebrew
experiment prices only the lexical mechanism, and prices it at the extreme
setting of total replacement.  The Greek experiment prices real imitation but
only at the intensity Second Sophistic authors actually achieved, in a
language whose annotation is coarser than \bhsa{}, and against a training set
whose register classification is a scholarly judgment rather than a datum
(S6 Table reports the sensitivity to that judgment).  Neither experiment
prices sustained morphosyntactic archaizing \emph{in Hebrew}, which is the
quantity a critic of the Song of the Sea result would most want.  Simulating
it would require a model of what Classical Hebrew grammar an imitator could
reconstruct, which we do not have.

\textbf{The Greek transfer is an analogy, not a measurement of Hebrew.}  That
Greek imitators achieved a \GKattshift~yr displacement establishes that the
deep mechanism works in principle and gives its rough scale.  It does not
establish that a Hebrew scribe could achieve the same, and the argument that
Second Temple Judaism lacked the institutional apparatus is a historical claim
we assert rather than demonstrate.

\textbf{One database, one text tradition.}  All Hebrew results depend on the
\bhsa{} annotation of the Masoretic text.  Consonantal variants in the
Qumran and Septuagint traditions are not represented, and the Masoretic
vocalisation reflects a much later stage of the language than any composition
date discussed here.  The features used are drawn from the consonantal text
and its morphological parse, but the parse itself is a modern scholarly
product.

\subsection*{Scholarly context for late Torah dating}

The finding that the Pentateuchal sources are post-exilic is not novel in
biblical scholarship, though it remains contested.  A substantial tradition
places the final composition of P in the Persian
period~\cite{Blenkinsopp1996,Nihan2007}, and the ``Persian period
Pentateuch'' position associated with the Copenhagen and Sheffield schools
places the whole compositional process
there~\cite{Davies1992,Lemche1993}.  Against this, Hurvitz's linguistic
argument for a pre-exilic P~\cite{Hurvitz1982,Hurvitz2014} and the broader
neo-documentary position maintain earlier dates.

The contribution here is not the direction of the result but that it arrives
with a calibrated uncertainty and a measured archaizing sensitivity.  The
linguistic argument for a pre-exilic P has always had to assume that the
post-exilic appearance of a text cannot be manufactured; the argument for a
post-exilic P has always had to assume the converse.  The measurements above
constrain both.

\subsection*{Extensibility}

The pipeline is language-agnostic given a morphologically annotated corpus and
a set of externally anchored dates.  The Greek replication was implemented
from the same code with a different feature extractor.  The binding
constraint is annotation, not method: Ugaritic, Phoenician and epigraphic
Hebrew would supply badly needed early anchors but lack comparable
morphological parsing.  Producing such a parse for the Iron Age epigraphic
corpus would be the single most valuable input to this line of work.

\subsection*{Relationship to authorship attribution}

Attribution and dating are complementary.  A method that assigns a text to a
scribal school and a method that assigns it a date constrain different axes of
the same question, and their errors are not the same errors.  A natural
extension is to use attribution output as a register covariate in the date
model, which would allow the genre confound documented above to be modelled
rather than merely reported.

% =====================================================================
\section*{Conclusion}
% =====================================================================

Biblical Hebrew morphosyntax carries a diachronic signal strong enough to
order books in time and to distinguish pre-exilic from post-exilic
composition, and too weak to resolve dates within the post-exilic period.
Applied to the Pentateuchal sources, a model calibrated on independently
anchored books places the Priestly, Deuteronomic and JE composites after the
exile with probability at least \srcminpost, and recovers the classical
relative sequence JE $\rightarrow$ D $\rightarrow$ P without having been
trained on any of them.  The Song of the Sea and the Song of Deborah are the
earliest of the \NTargets{} undated units.

The premise on which all such conclusions rest --- that a late author cannot
convincingly write early --- has been treated as an assumption for two
decades.  It is measurable, and measuring it shows that it is not one
assumption but two, with different answers.  Complete lexical archaizing of a
securely dated late Hebrew book buys a mean of \arcMean~yr of apparent
antiquity: the diagnostic vocabulary that the \cbh{}/\lbh{} literature treats
as the substance of archaizing turns out to carry very little of a
passage-level model's leverage.  The Second Sophistic Atticizers, who
reconstructed Classical grammar rather than Classical vocabulary and were
trained to do so by a formal curriculum, are displaced by \GKattshift~yr.

Archaizing therefore has a price, and the price is set by how deep the
imitation goes.  This is a more useful result than immunity would have been,
because it converts a rhetorical impasse into a comparison that can be made
case by case.  For any text whose date is disputed on linguistic grounds, the
question is no longer whether archaizing is possible in the abstract but
whether the compositional milieu in question supported the deep kind.  For the
Second Sophistic the answer is documented and affirmative.  For Second Temple
Judaism no comparable programme is attested, and the closest analogue --- the
Qumran sectarian scrolls, which mix Classical forms with Aramaisms rather than
sustaining a Classical grammar --- resembles the cheap mechanism rather than
the expensive one.
